evidence.claim: Across the Ouachita mountaintops, with a presidential dedication at Big Cedar
evidence.quote: The drive crosses the tops of the Ouachita Mountains

evidence.claim: a presidential dedication at Big Cedar
evidence.quote: President John F. Kennedy visited Big Cedar on October 29, 1961, to dedicate the opening of US-259, then called the Ouachita National Forest Road.

evidence.claim: Mountain Pass follows US 259 for 23 miles between Page and Octavia, crossing the tops of the Ouachita Mountains.
evidence.quote: The Mountain Pass Scenic Byway is located in southeast Oklahoma and follows Hwy 259 for 23 miles between Page and Octavia. The drive crosses the tops of the Ouachita Mountains

evidence.claim: It is a paved, two-lane drive with steep hills and curves.
evidence.quote: Both are two-lane paved roads with plenty of steep hills and curves

evidence.claim: Oklahoma’s tourism department presents the scenic byway as a route through the Winding Stair Mountain National Recreation Area, with wilderness, the Kerr Arboretum and access to the Ouachita National Recreation Trail.
evidence.quote: cuts through the 26,445-acre Winding Stair Mountain National Recreation Area. Wilderness areas and the Kerr Arboretum offer seclusion for hikers, backpackers and horseback riders. Visit the Ouachita National Recreation Trail for beautiful vistas that can be accessed from the byway.

evidence.claim: This road had a presidential opening: John F. Kennedy came to Big Cedar on October 29, 1961, to dedicate the route then called the Ouachita National Forest Road.
evidence.quote: President John F. Kennedy visited Big Cedar on October 29, 1961, to dedicate the opening of US-259, then called the Ouachita National Forest Road.

evidence.claim: A memorial dedicated in 1966 marks the US 259 and State Highway 63 intersection.
evidence.quote: A John F. Kennedy Memorial, dedicated in 1966, is at the intersection of US-259 with SH-63 in Big Cedar.

evidence.claim: The community itself predates the dedication: its post office opened in 1903, when Big Cedar lay in Wade County in the Choctaw Nation’s Apukshunnubbee District.
evidence.quote: A post office opened at Bigcedar, Indian Territory on April 3, 1903.

evidence.claim: Big Cedar lay in Wade County in the Choctaw Nation’s Apukshunnubbee District.
evidence.quote: At the time of its founding, Big Cedar was located in Wade County, a part of the Apukshunnubbee District of the Choctaw Nation.

evidence.claim: Driving south from the Page end, US 259 meets State Highway 1, the Talimena Drive, before reaching Big Cedar and State Highway 63.
evidence.quote: US-259 reenters the national forest north of this junction, and intersects SH-63 at Big Cedar. It then has a junction with SH-1, the Talimena Drive.

evidence.claim: The Kerr Arboretum is a separate forest excursion near the northern part of the drive.
evidence.quote: The area is bordered by U.S. 270-59 and Forest Road 6007 on the north and the Talimena Scenic Byway (east of U.S. 259) to the west and south.

evidence.claim: Continue through national forest toward the State Highway 144 junction near Octavia, the byway’s southern end.
evidence.quote: The U.S. route then serves as the eastern terminus of SH-144 near Octavia. US-259 reenters the national forest north of this junction

evidence.claim: Octavia, the byway’s southern end.
evidence.quote: follows Hwy 259 for 23 miles between Page and Octavia.

evidence.claim: Dwarf white oaks, yellow buckeye and Ouachita indigo distinguish the Kerr Arboretum’s plant communities.
evidence.quote: The arboretum features dwarf white oaks, yellow buckeye, Ouachita indigo, and grass seeps.

evidence.claim: The Robert S. Kerr Memorial Arboretum, Nature Center and Botanical Area covers 8,026 acres in the Ouachita National Forest near Talihina.
evidence.quote: The Robert S. Kerr Memorial Arboretum, Nature Center and Botanical Area is a 8,026 acres (32.48 km2) arboretum and nature preserve in the Ouachita National Forest, near Talihina, Oklahoma

evidence.claim: Its boundaries reach US 270-59 on the north and the Talimena Scenic Byway on the west and south.
evidence.quote: The area is bordered by U.S. 270-59 and Forest Road 6007 on the north and the Talimena Scenic Byway (east of U.S. 259) to the west and south.

evidence.claim: The tourism department includes the arboretum among the byway’s opportunities for hikers, backpackers and horseback riders.
evidence.quote: Wilderness areas and the Kerr Arboretum offer seclusion for hikers, backpackers and horseback riders.

evidence.claim: The junction of US 259 and State Highway 63 has a memorial to a road dedication attended by President John F. Kennedy.
evidence.quote: A John F. Kennedy Memorial, dedicated in 1966, is at the intersection of US-259 with SH-63 in Big Cedar.

evidence.claim: Kennedy visited on October 29, 1961, to open what was then called the Ouachita National Forest Road.
evidence.quote: President John F. Kennedy visited Big Cedar on October 29, 1961, to dedicate the opening of US-259, then called the Ouachita National Forest Road.

evidence.claim: The memorial was dedicated five years later, in 1966.
evidence.quote: A John F. Kennedy Memorial, dedicated in 1966

evidence.claim: Another route meets the community too: the Ouachita National Recreation Trail, with the Big Cedar trailhead at mile 30.5 of its second segment.
evidence.quote: Big Cedar is on the Ouachita National Recreation Trail, sometimes simply called the Ouachita Trail. The Big Cedar Trailhead is at mile 30.5 of Segment 02 of the Trail.

evidence.claim: Octavia takes its name from its first postmaster, Octavia Lewis.
evidence.quote: It took its name from Octavia Lewis, its first postmaster.

evidence.claim: The post office opened in Indian Territory on October 29, 1898, and closed in 1953.
evidence.quote: A post office was established at Octavia, Indian Territory on October 29, 1898.  It closed on September 30, 1953.

evidence.claim: At its founding, the community belonged to Nashoba County in the Choctaw Nation’s Apukshunnubbee District.
evidence.quote: At the time of its founding, Octavia was located in Nashoba County, a part of the Apukshunnubbee District of the Choctaw Nation.

evidence.claim: It remains an unincorporated community on the Choctaw Reservation and marks the end of this byway.
evidence.quote: Octavia is an unincorporated community on the Choctaw Reservation, in Le Flore County, Oklahoma, United States.

evidence.claim: marks the end of this byway.
evidence.quote: follows Hwy 259 for 23 miles between Page and Octavia.

evidence.claim: The recreation area encompasses 26,445 acres, and forested campgrounds lie a short drive off the byway.
evidence.quote: cuts through the 26,445-acre Winding Stair Mountain National Recreation Area.

evidence.claim: forested campgrounds lie a short drive off the byway.
evidence.quote: Several forested campgrounds are located a short drive off the byway.

evidence.claim: At Big Cedar, the Ouachita Trail adds a walking route to the highway crossing, with a named trailhead in the community.
evidence.quote: Big Cedar is on the Ouachita National Recreation Trail, sometimes simply called the Ouachita Trail. The Big Cedar Trailhead is at mile 30.5 of Segment 02 of the Trail.

evidence.claim: The older community’s postal name changed too: its office opened as Bigcedar in 1903, became Big Cedar in 1929 and closed in 1943.
evidence.quote: A post office opened at Bigcedar, Indian Territory on April 3, 1903.  On December 1, 1929, the official spelling of the post office name was changed to Big Cedar.  The post office was discontinued on October 15, 1943.

flags: The cache does not document the scenic designation date or formal criteria. Kennedy’s road dedication is kept distinct from byway designation.

Kerr Arboretum source contradicts itself on facilities: it lists toilets and trails but also says there are no developed recreation facilities and few signs. No facilities, driving-access or trail-condition promises made.
Octavia and Kerr Arboretum moments are concise because the cache offers little history or verified visitor detail.
Omitted the claim that Talimena Drive runs parallel to US 259: the tourism text says this, but the highway account establishes a junction and the geographic scope of parallel is unclear.
No primary transcript of Kennedy’s remarks is cached; the dedication is supported by the Big Cedar source, not an invented quotation.
